**IBM Watson for Oncology — a model that learned a few doctors’ habits (2013–2018)**

IBM sold Watson for Oncology as software that had read the cancer literature and could recommend treatments. By 2018 it was in use at more than 230 hospitals and had supported care for over 84,000 patients, according to STAT News, the publication that investigated it.

That July, STAT obtained internal IBM presentations documenting, in IBM’s own words, “multiple examples of unsafe and incorrect treatment recommendations” — advice conflicting with national guidelines, and one case in which a patient already suffering severe bleeding was recommended a drug that can cause fatal haemorrhage. A physician at Jupiter Hospital in Florida was blunt: “We can’t use it for most cases.” IBM said no patient was harmed.

The slides blamed the training. Rather than being fitted to real patient records, the system had been drilled by IBM engineers and a group of doctors at Memorial Sloan Kettering on a small number of “synthetic” cases — hypothetical patients the doctors invented. What went in was the preferences of a few clinicians at one hospital; what came out was the preferences of a few clinicians at one hospital, delivered with the authority of a machine said to have read everything.

That is this lesson’s mental model made concrete. A model is a function whose behaviour is decided by the data used to set its weights: training chooses the behaviour, inference only runs it again. Every LLM call runs a function whose knobs were fixed by one pile of text ending on one date — which is why there is a knowledge cutoff, and why a model can be confident about things it never saw.

**Caliskan, Bryson and Narayanan — measuring prejudice with nothing but a cosine (2017)**

In 2017 Aylin Caliskan, Joanna Bryson and Arvind Narayanan published a paper in *Science* with an uncomfortable finding. They took GloVe, an off-the-shelf set of word embeddings trained on roughly 840 billion tokens of web text, and applied no new machine learning at all. Their entire instrument was the measurement in this lesson: cosine similarity between vectors.

Their Word Embedding Association Test asks how close one set of words sits to another. Run on the plain GloVe vectors, it reproduced documented human biases: flower words sat nearer “pleasant” terms than insect words did; female names sat nearer family words and male names nearer career words; and names common among white Americans sat nearer pleasant terms than names common among Black Americans. A companion test went further — the gender association of fifty occupation words predicted the real proportion of women in those jobs in 2015 US Bureau of Labor Statistics data, with a correlation of 0.90.

Nobody labelled any of this. No one told the model that “nurse” was a woman’s job. The embedding was fitted to text, and the geometry of that text already carried the statistics of who had historically done what — accurately enough to predict a government table.

Hold on to that when you build with embeddings. The cosine you compute here is not a neutral window onto meaning; it reports where a training corpus placed a piece of text, regularities and all. A system that ranks chunks by cosine similarity inherits every pattern in the corpus its embedding model learned from, useful and ugly alike.

**University of Oxford — the same sentence, fifteen times the tokens (2023)**

At NeurIPS 2023, Aleksandar Petrov, Emanuele La Malfa, Philip Torr and Adel Bibi of the University of Oxford presented “Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages”. Their method was deliberately plain: take 2,000 sentences from FLORES-200 — a corpus in which the *same* sentences are professionally translated into over 200 languages — push them through 17 tokenisers including `cl100k_base`, the one behind ChatGPT and GPT-4, and count tokens.

Identical meaning, wildly different counts. For some language pairs the same sentence came out more than fifteen times longer in tokens. The cause is the mechanism this lesson describes: a tokeniser learns its sub-word chunks from a corpus dominated by English, so a well-represented language gets whole words in one token while a thinly-represented script is shredded into fragments, sometimes down to single bytes. The disparity, the authors note, arises before the model is invoked at all.

That matters because the token is three units at once: the billing unit, the latency unit and the context unit. A speaker of an unlucky language pays several times more for the same request, waits longer, and fits a fraction as much material into the same context window.

Take this as the practical form of “models read tokens, not words”. The familiar rule of thumb — one token is about four characters — is an *English* rule of thumb, and every cost estimate, context budget and truncation limit you set quietly assumes it. Count the tokens of the text you will actually send, in the language you will actually send it in.

**JFrog — the model file that ran a command the moment Python opened it (2024)**

In February 2024 the security research team at JFrog published the results of scanning the machine-learning models hosted on Hugging Face. Around 100 carried a real malicious payload. One, uploaded as `baller423/goober2`, opened a reverse shell to an attacker-controlled address the instant it was loaded — handing over remote control of the machine while the victim watched a model load normally.

The mechanism is ordinary Python. Model files of that kind are **pickles**, produced by Python’s `pickle` module. A pickle does not hold only data: a class can define a `__reduce__` method naming a callable and its arguments, to be run when the object is rebuilt. So `pickle.load` is not reading a file — it is executing instructions found inside it. The attacker broke nothing; they used the format as designed, hiding the payload in the trusted deserialisation step.

Compare that with `json.loads`, the parser this lesson gives you. JSON can only ever produce dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and null, and the worst a malformed one does is raise `JSONDecodeError` — which is why a `try/except` around it is enough. It is also why the AI ecosystem moved to **safetensors**, a format storing tensors and nothing executable.

The habit generalises. Model output, API responses and downloaded files all arrive as bytes from somewhere you do not control, and the discipline is the one you practise here: never assume the shape, parse defensively, handle the failure. Choosing *which* parser to reach for is part of it.

**Mercedes-Benz — one token in a public repository (2023–2024)**

On 29 September 2023 a Mercedes-Benz employee published a GitHub authentication token inside their own public repository. It sat there in the open for months. On 11 January 2024 researchers at RedHunt Labs came across it during a routine internet-wide scan for leaked credentials — not a targeted attack on the carmaker, but a net cast across GitHub that the token happened to fall into.

The token was unrestricted and unmonitored, and it unlocked the company’s internal GitHub Enterprise server. As reported by TechCrunch, which helped notify the company, anyone holding it could have reached source code, API keys, cloud access keys, database connection strings, design documents, blueprints and single sign-on passwords. Mercedes-Benz was told on 22 January 2024, confirmed the exposure, and revoked the token two days later.

Nothing exotic happened. A credential was written where code lives and pushed to a public remote. The properties that make Git so useful — a permanent record of everything, handed in full to anyone who clones — are precisely what make it the worst place to keep a secret. Deleting the file in a later commit does not help: the old commit still holds it, and automated scanners read new public commits within minutes.

So the order of operations in this lesson matters more than it looks. Write a `.gitignore` containing `.env` *before* your first commit, keep the key in the environment, and read it at runtime with `os.getenv`. A generative-AI key spends real money on your card, which puts you in the position Mercedes-Benz was in — without the security researchers who eventually found it.
